prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

That is, high traffic volume is similarly evaluated as arterial roads regarding Mental Comfort, Interaction, and Environment, but more negative regarding the Ease of Use and, in particular, Physical Comfort. This suggest that the evaluation of the residential road might be positive due to the lower traffic volume, but still, at resi- dential roads, cyclists need to interact with others, need to give priority, or at least cycle carefully which leads to lower ratings in Mental Comfort, Interaction, and Physical Comfort. Regarding the various cycling facilities, the separated cycle path is rated the best on all clusters, directly followed by the adjacent cycle path, and the cycle lane. Interestingly, at the separated cycling facility, all clusters have almost the same ratings, except the Environment cluster. That is, although cyclists ride in an unpleasant surrounding with noises and exhausts, a separated cycling facility leads to high Mental Comfort because cyclists have their own road space and feel safe, they do not need to interact with others, the markings and signs are clear and easy to use, and the Physical Comfort is high because nothing hinders the cyclists to cycle their own speed. This is even more the case for cycle paths that separate more strictly from motor traffic than just by a curb and that also separated from the pedestrian traffic. The preference of separation from motor traffic has been found in many studies (e.g., Skov-Petersen et al., 2018; von Stülpnagel & Binnig, 2022), but it is interesting to see that the attention due to interaction increases, and that the Mental Comfort and the pleas- antness of the environment decreased as soon as the cycle facility runs on the road level. Even at the cycle lane which is still clearly separated by lane markings, Mental Comfort is lower than on physically separated paths. Still, it is higher than on arterial or residential streets, but in order to offer cycling infrastructure that can be used relaxed and stress-free, planners should decide for physically separated cycle paths if possible. The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"

1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).

The evaluation of low traffic volume, on the other hand, is even more positive than the residential road, especially on Physical Comfort. This suggest that the evaluation of the residential road might be positive due to the lower traffic volume, but still, at resi- dential roads, cyclists need to interact with others, need to give priority, or at least cycle carefully which leads to lower ratings in Mental Comfort, Interaction, and Physical Comfort. Regarding the various cycling facilities, the separated cycle path is rated the best on all clusters, directly followed by the adjacent cycle path, and the cycle lane. Interestingly, at the separated cycling facility, all clusters have almost the same ratings, except the Environment cluster. That is, although cyclists ride in an unpleasant surrounding with noises and exhausts, a separated cycling facility leads to high Mental Comfort because cyclists have their own road space and feel safe, they do not need to interact with others, the markings and signs are clear and easy to use, and the Physical Comfort is high because nothing hinders the cyclists to cycle their own speed. This is even more the case for cycle paths that separate more strictly from motor traffic than just by a curb and that also separated from the pedestrian traffic. The preference of separation from motor traffic has been found in many studies (e.g., Skov-Petersen et al., 2018; von Stülpnagel & Binnig, 2022), but it is interesting to see that the attention due to interaction increases, and that the Mental Comfort and the pleas- antness of the environment decreased as soon as the cycle facility runs on the road level. Even at the cycle lane which is still clearly separated by lane markings, Mental Comfort is lower than on physically separated paths. Still, it is higher than on arterial or residential streets, but in order to offer cycling infrastructure that can be used relaxed and stress-free, planners should decide for physically separated cycle paths if possible. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. EET REFINED CONSTRUCTION GUIDELINES 2. Vehicle Traffic System 2 Vehicle Traffic System 2.1 Vehicle Traffic Space Scale The longitudinal and transverse road space occupied by vehicular traffic is referred to as vehicle traffic space. Generally speaking, vehicle traffic space includes carriageways, bus-only lanes, medians, and roadside parking lanes. Figure 2.1-1 Components of Vehicle Traffic Space 2.1.1 Motor Vehicle Lane The width of a motor vehicle lane shall include the carriageway width and the curb lane widths on both sides. Where a single carriageway road or a three-carriageway road uses a central separator or double yellow lines to separate opposing traffic, the pavement width of the motor vehicle lane shall also include the width of the separator or double yellow lines. 1. Running Lane The width of a running lane is related to the road design speed. The recommended width for urban road running lanes is 3.25 m–3.5 m. 2. Two-Way Single Lane Where a lower-grade branch road is designed as a single lane permitting two-way travel, the width shall be 4.5 m. The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. At bus stops, the lane width shall be 3 m. 27 Figure 2.1-2 Typical Lane Width Settings 2.1.2 Tidal Lane In response to the “tidal phenomenon” of traffic, lanes may be provided on road sections whose direction of travel can be changed according to traffic flow demand. In addition, the control center may monitor intersection conditions through instruments and, when appropriate, use remote control means to control signboards; where intersection signal controllers are connected in a computer network, they may also be identified through an automatic recognition system and automatically regulated. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces.
